A misses, reads revision 1 from the source and stores its own card. A returns GBP 20.00. B is still empty.
B misses despite A’s earlier fill. It reads the source and stores another copy, expiring ten seconds after A’s. B returns GBP 20.00.
The source now has revision 2. This comparison deliberately uses expiry alone, so neither local copy changes yet.
A’s copy has expired. A reads revision 2 and fills its local cache, returning GBP 22.00. B still holds revision 1.
B hits its own unexpired copy and returns GBP 20.00, after A returned GBP 22.00. Separate expiry times allow different answers.

B hits the copy A just filled and returns GBP 22.00. This history saved a source read, but every request made a remote cache lookup.

Both applications share one cache. Start with a cache miss.
App A reads revision 1 from the source. It has the old price in memory but has not copied it into the cache.
App B commits revision 2. App A still holds the answer it read before that commit.
App B deletes the key. Deletion succeeds even though App A has not filled it yet.
App A creates the key with revision 1. Deletion removed the key, but did not remove App A’s saved answer or its ability to fill.

The database owns P7’s price. The cache has no copy of its product card.
The first request asks for P7. App A looks for its card in the cache. A missing entry is a cache miss.
App A reads the product from the source and builds the display card. The cache does not fetch the product itself.
App A saves the card under its key and returns it. Saving the copy is called filling the cache.
The next request finds the saved card: a cache hit. App A returns it without reading the source. The source-read count stays at one.
Start with P7’s card already cached. No request in this drawing overlaps the update.
The source has accepted GBP 22.00. Its commit does not change the separate cached copy, which still says GBP 20.00.
After the commit, App A deletes the card. Deletion ends reuse without needing to build the replacement immediately.
The next product request misses and reads revision 2 from the source.
App A fills the cache with revision 2. Later requests can reuse the new price.

The source and both cache copies agree on revision 1. Replication has caught up at this starting point.
The source commits GBP 22.00 at revision 2. Neither cached copy has changed yet.
The primary applies DEL and replies successfully. Its replica has not received the deletion. The two cached states now differ.
The primary fails before the deletion reaches the replica. After promotion and client reconnection, the new endpoint still holds revision 1.
App A reads GBP 20.00 from the new primary. For a read requiring revision 2 or newer, this is an unusable hit. The source path still needs admission and remaining time.

Two dots move to v2: ten requests. Its empty namespace misses on all ten. Add nine misses from v1: nineteen source reads, inside the thirty-start allowance.
The useful v2 entries now produce hits. Total demand work returns to ten reads. Check latency, errors and answer validity before increasing traffic.

The old format still decodes, but its invalidation path stopped. Refuse these untrusted copies and rebuild through the source gate. One hundred requests now want reads: thirty are admitted, seventy refused. Pause the rollback and recover gradually.
The first caller asks App A for P7. Redis holds no copy yet.
The missing key is a cache miss. App A must obtain the card from its source.
App A admits this source read. If the source budget were full, the request would be refused here.
The source has answered. App A now owns the result it will return; saving a copy is a separate operation.
One SET stores both the value and its expiry. The next reader can reuse this copy.
